England can never become a great continental power: even if it were possible, the atininirent of such would be foreign to her objects and interests: her dominion is on the ocean þÿ with her ileets and colonies she can c tnnnand and control, as she has before done, the coasts and commerce of all who may proclaim themselves her enemies. But in no instance has England ever waged an offensive war in Europe; whenever she has been provoked into contests, it has either been lor the maintenance of her principles, or in self defence. France may desire to extend her boundaries to the Rhine, Spain to reannex Portugal to the ancient thrones of Castile and Arragon: Austria avariciously graps Italy; Russia daily augments her t rritories from the dislocated provinces of Turkey; but England seeks no'hiug in Europe. Whatever may be the extent of her acquisitions in other parts of the globe, the white nations have assuredly no reason to fear an encroachment on their territories and rights; and In the extension of her colonies a nong the dark coloured races of the tropics, she is cheapening the luxuries of life, and enabling all Europe to profit by her exertions. Nations should be above the petty jealousies of shopkeepers in provincial towns. The merchant of an expansive and just mind, feels that it is for his interest to have rich and enterprising neighbours, whether at home or abroad. Thus also it is with kingdoms; whatever improvement England produces in

tiie manufacture of cotton, silk, wool, &,c., or in t ie preparation of machinery, Europe soon feels the benefit of her skill and capital, and, without the previous labour and expense, derives the full measure of advantage from her insular neighbour. We have thus shown that there is no just ground for the hostility which the continental powers have expressed towards England ; and our future pages will develope how little England has to dread from the united hostility of every nation of Europe, were it possible for them all to combine against her. 1'oreigners never comprehend sufficiently our social state or internal resources. If, by any madness, England were to be plunged into war, party feeling would soon subsid and the , energies of this mighty country would be put fuxib with tremendous effect. We should, as before strip every hostile nation of their colonies, sweep the seas of their vessels, and blockade their coasts. Autocrats or despotic sovereigns would soon find that their domestic condition would not be favourable to the maintenance of their present power; and that which would but Consolidate our internal strength, would, if necessity required it, be made an instrument for breaking their rule. We desire not to dwell on this subject, and have not the least intention of using minatory lmguage ; on the contrary, we wish to prove that it is the interest of every nation in Europe to he at peace with England, and it is for their direct personal good that she should maintain her colonial power and oceanic
s ipremacy; and when we come to discuss, at a future period, our political and coinmeicial relations with our European brethren, we shall endeavour to show how little England

®A»3JR ' 'Ta3Ma»333t þÿ« irS'-MIT 8 has to fear or to care for the hostility or friendship ofiier Continental neighbours, apart from those general considerations which we trust will ever sway a Christian kingdom. There will arise so many occasions for an examination of each and all the points adverted to, and for a minute inquiry into the basis of our structure, as the oldest kingdom on the earth, that we pass on to shadow forth a brief vaticination of the future prospects ol England Two proceedings, now in their infancy, are destined to exercise a most important influence on the future condition ol this empire : the one is, the stream of emigration in the direction of the Southern Bole; the other, the flow of our commerce towards the Eastern Hemisphere ; the one containing millions of acres, in a genial clime, ready for the plough ; the other, myraids ol comparatively civilized men, ready to supply in exchange lor our manufactures, all the valuable and varied products, of the tropics. These two circumstances, in connexion with a sound monetary and fhc.nl system at home, will make England young again, with all the wisdom of mature age, and all the benefits of advancing science and accumulated capital. There will thus be a new spring to her existence ; whatever she has before accomplished will be trifling compared to her future efforts ; and with 28,000,000 of free, educated, industrious, and religious inhabii ants at home, this small island in the German Ocean, will hold complete sway over the entire Eastern world.

Nor will the Western or American hemisphere be neglected ; our possessions in the Northern and Southern portions of that continent, on its Atlantic and Faeific coasts ; and the rich islands < >t its tropical seas, under the stimulus of personal freedom and constitutional liberty, will yet add materially to our resources, populaiion, and power : and when the immense advantages of the vast countries watered by the Oiinoco and Amazon are developed, England will be prepared to participate in their enjoyment. While our native land is intersected with railways, the wide ocean will be traversed by our steam vessels, reducing the distance of months to weeks, and connected by our floating bridges the continents of both hemispheres. Sooner or later, the1 Anglo-Saxon language will become the universal medium for communication between foreign nations, and thus give to England a perpetual presence and identification with those who now perhaps deem themselves our rivals. By the aid of machinery, physical toil will be lessened, man, in ceasing to be a machine, will become more and more an intellectual being, and, with a full perception of the duties as well as the enjoyments of lile, political privileges mav be gradually conceded, and the progress of society will be equable and happy. England, evert now, may claim the designation of the queen mother of nations ; by a just policy, the offspring of her loins will become the sinews of her strength, until, like the banyan tree of the East, every fibre and

shoot more and more effectually shields, up. holds, and adorns the parent stem. Amidst the thousand million of human beings that now inhabit the earth (independent of the myriads it is still capable of containing). there cannot be one uninterested in the fulure progress of England, it England act up to the Christian principles which are the louudaliou of her religion Those princi-

S3 AV13 ples are the preservation of peace, the liberation of the slave, the judicious extension ot rational freedom, and the permanent establishment of Christianity. It was doubtless for these great and holy objects that this small island has been permitted to rise from a barbarian colony of heathen Rome, where her children was sold as slaves, to her present exalted state ; and if she be but true to the 'dictates of that divine creed which has been revealed to man for his temporal as well as spiritual welfare, we cannot contemplate an end to her power, nor a boundary toiler happiness. It is not, therefore, for the sake of the small territori d speak called Britain, that we seek the extension and the permanence of her supremacy ; it is because we believe that the destinies of mankind are intimately blended with her weal or woe, and that an awful responsibility rests upon t he course w hich, in the exercise of a free agency, she may for the future pursue. Cheerfully do we confess, that we feel no gloomy forebodings; there are within even this small island too many good Christians to suffer despair to creep with its noisome weeds around the heart ; we believe that the salt of the earth is in Britain, and that it contains the little heaven which will yet leaven the entire mass of mankind þÿ among whom our revered ministers are everywhere spreading the light of a pure gospel, and preaching its comforts and blessings in every known tongue. Finally, we desire to he actively useful in

aiding towuds the fulfilment of the high behests to which we believe England is called: we wish to cast our mile into the genera) treasury for the ad' anc nient of human happiness þÿ and. invoking the blessing ol the good upon our labours, wiili pel feet confidence we commit the result to the disposal of that Almighty Providence wlu> watched over and goverm th the universe.

The foreign intelligence of the week is not of much importance. The affairs of the East are still unsettled ; the French government quietly, but still firmly, taking the part of JVIehetnel Ali, so far as to support his pretensions to an hereditary government in Egypt, and to his retention of a considerable part, if not the whole of Syria. The secret purpose of France in so doing is, certainly, a little covert jealousv of England, and an apprehen- | Queens sion that Egypt, if left weak and dependent, mav fall too much under British influence, and may become her immediate conquest in the event of war. On the other hand, the English government, having a more just apprehension of the power of Russia, just as quietly and firmly in its own turn, is taking the part of Turkey, and insists that the separation of Syria from Turkey would at once render that monarchy incapable of her own defence, and would violate the principle of maintaining the integrity of the Ottoman empire. Under these circumstances Russia, as if watching for the event, takes no decided part with either of the two powers, except that of opposing the objects of England in an underhanded manner. It is difficult to say how all this will end, hut it is understood that each of the three powers deems it necessary to augment the force of iis own respective fleets upon the Egy ptian and Mediterranean stations We have only to repeat our own former view of what appears to us to he the right line of policy ; let us do what we can in

Sir þÿ I have the honor to announce to you that Mr Stipendiary Magistrate Pedder, who was commissioned to proceed to Anguilla in compliance with your Excellency's instructions of 25th tilt., has this morning returned from that Island.

The tide of emigration seems for a time to have stopped, and I confess that it would afibrd me sincere pleasure if any other means could be adopted, before the necessity for Emigration again occurs, for rescuing Anguilla from its unfortunate condition as a Colony I cannot but believe that if, in accordance with your Excellency's suggestion, a responsible President were appointed, that such proof of the solicitude of Her Majesty's Government for the welfare of the Colony would be attended with the happiest effect, that the mere presence of such an officer would tend to restore confidence, that capital would be embarked, and the lands be brought again into cultivation. 1 have lately had an opportunity of conversing with several persons who are likely to be well informed on the subject, who are of opinion, that there is a large quantity of land in Anguilla capable of producing abundant crops of Sugar of the finest qualitv. Mr. Pedder further reports that many of the labouring class said to him, that if a regular sugar Estate were established, such as they had elsewhere seen, decent Cottages built, and fair wages paid, not only would emigration cease, but that most of those who had already emigrated would be happy to return to their native Island. At present there is no public spirit, no confidence, no protection for property, and consequently even those residents w ho do possess Capital are afraid, or unwilling to turn it to any account by sugar cultivation. But I have so lately conferred

with your Excellency on this subject, and so fully concur in those views which you were please to communicate to me, that I will trouble you w ith no further remark. Mr Pedder is of opinion that the Population even now numbers not less than 250 White, 250 colored, and about 1000 labouring people. Surely with such a population and a fertile soil, it would not be difficult for a responsible President, residing on the spot, to take steps which might avail, not only to save Anguilla from depopulation, but to place it on
a respectable footing as a Colony of Great Britain I have, &c. (Signed) U. T. Cunningham. Lieut. Governor, His Excellency, The Governor of the Leeward Islands.

GALVESTON. This place is becoming quite important in a commercial view. There are three steam ships plying between it and New Orleans, and packet lines of brigs and schooners to Baltimore, Philadelphia, New York and \ew Orleans, besides eignt or ten smaller vessels plying between the city and the towns on the neighboring rivers; and it is stated that between the 1st of December and 1st of May, the number of foreign arrivals exceeded one hundred and fifty.

At the time of the last war between this country and Great Britain, Galveston island was the head quarters of Lafitte, the celebrated French pirate, who built, there two or three houses; and only three years ago there were but five or six houses on the whole island. At present it is said to contain within the city not less than 900 buildings, among which are two churches, many large warehouses and commodious hotels.
The morals of the place are favorably spoken of by the Rev. Mr. M'Calla, formerly ol this city ; and it is probably one of the most salubrious residences in the world.

þÿ » ooo DISCOVERY OF MUMMIES AT DU- RANGO, MEXICO. A million of mummies, it is staled, have lately been discovered in the environs of Durango, in Mexico. They are in a sitting posture, but have the wrappings, bands, ornaments of the Egyptian. An ng them was found a poniard of flint, with a sculptured handle, chaplets, necklaces, and of alternately colored beads, fragments of bones polished like ivory, hue worked clastic tissues (probably our modern India rubber cloth,) mocassins worked like those of our Indians to day, bones of vipers, tttc. It remains to continue these interesting researches, and Ameri ca will become another Egypt to antiquarians, and her ruins will go back to the oldest periods of the world, showing doubtless that the ancestors of the Monlezurnas lived on the Nile, and that their luxurious civilization was broken up and overpowered by the hardy hordes of Asiatic Tartars, who came down from Behring s Straits and the Rocky Mountains. The scenes of Attila and Alaric in Rome and Greece, were rehearsed at an earlier day on the shores of California and the plain of Mexico. It is unknown of tiie mummies above mentioned what kind of embalmment was used, or whether it was nitrous depositions in the caves where they were found. A fact of importance is stated, that the shell of the necklaces are of a marine shell found at Zacatecas, on the Pacific, where the Columbus of their forefathers probably therefore landed from the Malay, Hindoostan or Chinese coast, from islands on the Indian ocean. þÿ Jamaica Morning Journal,

WOOD PAVEMENT IN LONDON. The following is taken from a London paper by the last packet : þÿ ' This article has now been laid down in the carriage-way of Oxford street for a period of sixteen months; and, on an average, 7000 vehicles, from 400 to 10 000 lbs. weight each, and 12,000 horses, have passed over it daily, notwithstanding which, scarcely any appearance of wear or change is perceptible on the surface It presents a uniform level, by which the draught, as on tramroads, is diminished to an extent that it is computed one horse would draw on these roads an equal burden to that which would require four on ordinary ones. Its noiseless quality, added to its freeness from mud and dust, are also strong recommendations to its use in public and trading thoroughfares. The adoption of this material for carriage-ways by the Marylebone vestry seems to have met with more than ordinary encouragement, thev having determined on covering another 4000 feet of Oxford street with wood paving, upon which workmen were employed on Saturday. þÿ They have also in contemplation to lay down wooden blocks as a carriage way paving the whole of the places of worship throughout the parish, that the devotion of the frequenters may not be disturbed during the service, or the thoroughfares near them stopped up, as in the Strand, to the inconvenience and annoyance of persons travelling through that locality. During the past week workmen have been employed in laying down wood paving near the Foundling Hospital. The inhabitants of Coventry street and Piccadilly

have applied to the parochial authorities of St. James's for wood pavement to be laid down in that extensive thoroughfare, upon the same principle as that laid down by order o! the Woods and Forests in Whitehall. þÿ This is on the same principle about to be laid down in Oxford street and Marvlebone, entitled the stereotomy of the cube, which brings into play principles greatly superior to t he rude mode of the wood paving on its first introduction. To carry out the principle, the blocks are cut on the level and cioss the street in rows, each alternate block leaning to the north, and the other in the contrary direction, so that when pinned together and abutted against the kirb on either side of the road, they form a self-supporting bridge, and a correct level is at the same time obtained, whi h has the effect of rendering it less slippery than it otherwise would be under a damp atmosphere. The demand for this description of wood paving has become so general that the proprietors of the patent have found it an affair of great difficulty to procure prepair J material in sufficient quantity, and have thus been subject to large fines for the non-performance of their contract. þÿ This has compelled them to seek out extraordinary means to prevent such serious consequences again resulting. <

f >om the New York Commercial Advertiser , July 20, 1840. Arrival of the. Britannia. FROM LIVERPOOL. At 9 o'clock this morning we received, by Harden's Boston express, our letters and papers brought by the new steam ship Britannia. Captain Ewing. Our London papers are to the evening of the 3d of July, and Liverpool to the 4th, both inclusive, with commercial lists to the latest date. The britannia left Liverpool on the afternoon of the 4th of July, and was only twelve days in reaching Halifax. She was telegraphed at Boston on Saturday evening at half past 7 o'clock, and was at her berth at East Boston at half past 9 o'clock, being the fourteenth day from her leaving Liverpool. þÿ She had eighty five passengers, sixty of whom were for the United States. Among them is the Hon Samuel Cunard, the enterprising proprietor of this new line. We learn that the next steam ship of this line will leave Liverpool on the 4th of August. The principal intelligence by this arrival is from the East, of which we give ample details below. In Parliament nothing of importance was done. A petition from Edinburgh was presented by 1 -oid Brougham, signed by 10,000 inhabitants, and praying for a dissolution of the connexion between Church and state. The election for sheriffs of the city of London terminated on the 1st of July, in the choice of the Conservative candidates. Alderman Gibbs and Mr. Earn comb. A great dispute was raging in the London papers on the question whether there were or were not balls in the pistol which Oxford fired at the Queen No bullets had been found.

Oxford's great-grand father was a black, and served in the royal navy. His grand father was a mulatto, and his father of course a quadroon. Don Carlos has published an " appeal to Europe," in the Augsburgh Gazette, against " an atrocious calumny" which he says the French government has circulated respecting him, that he had entertained a project of poisoning the young Queen and her mother, and generally against his treatment in France. The Paris journals positively announce the recall of Marshal Vallee from Algiers, and the appointment of Marshal Molitor to succeed him.

State of Birmingham. To give anything like a correct picture of the depressed state of trade in Birmingham, and its consequences, would be no easy matter. The oldest, most extensive and respectable merchants, manufacturers and traders, concur in representing the present depression as unprecedented in their experience. Ten thousand applications by working men and women, for free passages to Australia, have been made and refused, within the last two months, at one emigration office in the town Between 20 and 30 good houses and retail shops are untenanted in three of the principal streets, and thousands of middle and small rented houses are' unoccupied in every part of the borough.

The walls are literally covered daily with auction bills, and a purchaser can hardly be found for either leasehold or freehold property. The pawnbrokers, being completely stocked, refuse any except what are termed best pledges. Thousands of mechanics are living on half wages, thousands on quarter wages, and numbers of creatures are sustained by means known only to the Almighty him- I self. Upward of 300 applications were made to the Gloucester Railway Company for situations as guards, otc., within the last month. þÿ The poor-rate is doubled, and numbers are leaving their houses to escape paying it. All is gloomy, and no one can see a prospect of improvement. In the midst of these symptoms of distress we have an apparent anomaly. Every where in the outskirts streets are being laid out, and houses rising as if by magic þÿ Birmingham Jour nal o f July 1.

From the London Sun of July 3. NEWS FROM CHINA. The overland mail from India has arrived, bringing Canton papers of the 27th of March, Singapore papers of the 15th of April, and Bombay papers of the 23d of May, inclusive. From Canton the news is more interesting than important. The Chinese were making (for them) vigorous preparations for hostilities with England They were busily constructing numerous fire-rafts for burning British shipping, and as from time immemo rial the ingenuity of the Chinese has been directed to the manufacture ol fire works' there is more danger to be apprehended from these infernal machines than from any of Admiral Kwan's floating batteries. The American merchants, finding that Canton was likely to be soon too hot for them and that Great Britain was not to be deterred from seeking reparation for the insult offered to the representative of her Sovereign, and the robbery of her subjects, by their protests, had quitted the provincial city, which put a complete stop to all foreign trade. The Druid, of 14 guns, had been ordered to join the squadron destined to make war on China. News of the death of the Empress of China had reached Canton. Pekin was said to be in a stale of dangerous excitement ; the stoppage of the foreign trade having occasioned great distress among the tea-growers and rhubarb cultivators. A considerable loss of revenue was experienced in the Imperial exchequer, and the mandarins who indirectly profited by the trade, were all discontented þÿ Bombay, Mav 9 þÿ

and discontent sometimes finds a tongue even under the despotic sway of the Imperial ruler of " ten thousand kingdoms." The reigning dynasty, being of the Tartar race, is exceedingly unpopular in China, and it is not impossible that the contest with England may lead to a revolution.

PITC AIRN'S ISLAND. Who has not heard of l'itcairn's Island, in the Pacific Ocean þÿ the solitary spot which Fletcher Christian, at the head of the mutineers of the Bounty, and their twany wives>

selected as an asylum, and there planted a colony? The history of this colony is one of the most interesting pieces of veritable narrative now þÿextant and proves that truth is stranger than fiction We have collected from various quarters some facts relating to the inhabitants of this island þÿ which have enabled us to present our readers with an article of considerable length, but which we believe many will deem highly interesting. In the year 1788. the ship Bounty, Capt. Bligh, s ailed from England, for the islands in the Pacific Ocean, for the purpose of procuring a quantity of plants of the bread fruit and other tropical trees, to be introduced into the English West India Islands. He arrived at Otaheite, one ol the Society Islands, on the 26th of September. He remained there for twenty-three weeks, and with his whole crew was treated with much affection and regard by the natives þÿ wnich seemed to iucrease in proportion to their star The women ot Olaiicite wore represented by Capt. Biigh as being handsome, rnilu, and cheerful in their manners and conversation þÿ and possessed of sufficient delicacy to make them admired mid beloved. And it is not surprising that a set ot sailors, most ol them void of connections, should form tender ties with these South Sea Islanders þÿ and regret to quit a place like Otaheile, where they had the power of fixing themselves in one ot the finest islands in the world, in the midst of plenty, where there was no occasion to labor, and where the

allurements of dissipation are beyond any conception that can be formed ol them. Accordingly after the Bounty had sailod from Otaheile þÿ having on board one thousand bread-fruit plants þÿ a plan was concerted among portion a of the officers and crew, to take possession ol the ship, and return to the island. The chief of the mutineers was Fletcher Christian, a young man and master's mate of the Bounty, i'lie whole plan was managed w ith great adroitness, and was completely successful. A few weeks after the ship left Otaheae, the mutineers took posession without any struggle or opposition þÿ pot Capt. Bligh, ami some of his officers, and a portion of the crew into the long boat, supplied thein vvitii provisions, and some other necessaries, and set them adrift. The boat, alter a perilous voyage ol many days, reached an island in the vicinity of i\ew HollanU þÿ and Capt. Bligii subsequently succeeded in reaciung England in safety. Meanwhile Cnristian mid his comrades returned in the Bounty to Otaheite, and there abandoned themselves to pleasure. But Christian had sense enough to know tnat as soon as the circumstances of the mutiny were known in England, a vessel would be despatched to arrest the mutineers. Jrle therefore urged his companions to embark with him 111 the Bounty, and with their Oiaheitcan wives seek a safe asylum in some other land. A part of them listened to his advice, and left the island Those who remained were a few mouths afterward shot down or captured by the crew of a British ship, sent out

b_> the British government for that purpose The beuutilul and solitary spot, called Fitcairn's island, was first discovered by Capt. Carteret, on the 4th of J uly, 1767 þÿ who says : " Upon approaching it from a distance, it first appears like a girt rock rising out of the sua. It is no inore than five miles in circunileienee, (now known to he 6 miles long and II broad) and uninhabited, It was, however,

covered with trees, and we saw a small stream of fresh water running down the side of it. i would have landed upon it, but the surl at that season of the year was so high as to render it impossible 1 got soundings at the west side of it, at somewhat less than a mile from t lie shore, in 25 fathoms, with a bottom of coral and sand. It lies in lat. 25 2 .South, long. 133 21 West þÿ and about 300 miles Westward of the continent of America. It was so high that we saw it at the distance of fifteen leagues." This island, from being situated far from the common track of navigation, remained unvisited from the time of its first discover, till the year 1790, when Fletcher Christian, the chief of the mutineers of the Bounty, after examining a number of islands in this part of the Pacific, in search of a retired and unin habited island, where he, with his comrades and their wives, might secrete themselves and end their days, fixed upon this island. He accordingly ran the ship þÿashore broke her up, auer taking out every thing valuable, and with a few Englishmen, the companions of his crime, and some Otaheitan men and women, established himself on this island. Ten years afterward, Christian was Killed by one of the Otaheitans þÿ and a few years after this circumstance, the Otaheitan men, instigated by jealousy, rose upon the English and killed all but one, named Alexander Smith, who fortunately escaped, and succeeded in concealing himself. On the following night, the women rose upon their countrymen, and

in turn killed them all þÿ and thus the Englishman, Smith, and seven Otaheitan women, were all of the original settlers who were left alive on the island. From that time, although several ships passed the island, none attempted to effect a landing, until the year 1808, when the ship Topaz, of Boston, owned by J. and T. H. Perkins, and commanded by Captain Mahew 1 olner, touched at the place. The Topaz was bound on a sealing voyage in the Pacific, and Captain Folger was induced to suppose \ from the situation of Pitcairn's island, that these animals might abound there þÿ and therefore determined to visit it and effect a landing- It had been described by former navigators as uninhabited þÿ and he was therefore much surprised perceive on nearing the island, a to canoe pulling off to the ship þÿ and much more so, when the men in the-canoe, one of whom was a son of Fletcher Christian, addressed him in good English, asking who he was, where he was from, &c. They went on boaid the Topaz and spent a short time, when Captain Folger accepted their invitation to accompany them on shore. The account of his interview with Smith is exceedingly inteþÿresting but too long to be given here entire We shall give a few passages, embodying | some interesting observations made by Capi tains Delano and Folger. Captain Folger remarked that Smith had taken great pains to educate the inhabitants of the island in the faith and principles of Christianity þÿ they were in the uniform practice of evening and morning prayer, and were

regularly assembled on Sundays for religious instruction and worship. The library and stationary of the Bounty furnished them with the means of considerable learning. Smith had improved himself greatly by the efforts he was obliged to make to instruct those under his carc. He wrote and conversed extremely well, and his journal was so hand-

somely kept as to attract particular attention þÿ and to excite regret that there was not time to copy it. The houses in the village were uncommonly neat. Tney were built after the manner of Otaheitans þÿ small trees were felled and cut into suitable lengths þÿ then driven into the ground, and interwoven with split bamboo. They were thatched with the leaves of the plantain and coeoanut, and the ground neatly covered with mats, very tastefully wrought. The young men labored in the fields and gardens, or employed themselves in different kinds of manufactures, such as canoes, household furniture, implements of agriculture, and apparatus for fishing. The girls made cloth of the bark of a tree, and attended to the domestic labors. They were cheerful, and as industrious, healthy, and beautiful, as they were temperate and simple in their habits. þÿ The provisions set before Captain Folger consisted of fowls, pork, and vegetables, cooked with great neatness and uncommonly well. The fruits were also excellent. The apron and shawl, worn by the girls, weie made from the bark of the cloth tree. This is taken from the trunk, and beaten till it is thin and soft and fit for use. Its natural color is buff", but it is dyed of various colors, as red, blue, or black þÿ and is sometimes covered with the figures of animals. When Smith was asked by Captain F. if he wished his existence to remain a secret, he replied " No," and, pointing to a young and blooming band by whom he was surrounded, the descendants of Christian and

his companions, continued, " Do you think any man could seek my life with such a picture as this before his eyes V When Captain F. was about to leave the island, the people pressed around him with the greatest affection and courtesy. The chronometer of the Bounty was given him as a present þÿ although of gold, it was so black with smoke and dust that the metal could hardly be discovered The girls brought him some presents of cloth, which they had made with their own hands, and which they had dyed with beautiful colors. Their unaffected and amiable manners, and their earnest prayer for his welfare, made a deep impression on iiis mind. Captain Folger made as suitable return of presents as was in his power, and left this most interesting community, with the keenest sensations of regret. It reminded him of Paradise, he said, more than any eff-rt of poetry or imagination. F.tcairn's island was again visited, Sept. 17, 1814, by Sir Thomas Staines, and Capt. Pipon, of the English Government ships Briton and Tagns ; and the latitude was ascertained to be 25 deg. 4 mm S. and 130 deg# 25 West. The description given by Sir Thomas of the island and its inhabitants is quite interesting, and fully confirms all that was said by Captain Folger. He says this interesting new colony consisted of about 46 persons, mostly grown up young people besides a number of infants. þÿ The young men, all born on the island, were very athletic, and of the finest forms þÿ their countenances open and pleasing, indicating

j much benevolence and goodness of heart þÿ but the yotfng women were objects of peculiar admiration þÿ tall, robust, and beautifully fn n cii, their faces beaming with smiles and un- | ruffled good humor þÿ but wearing a degree of

iBAirsjs modesty that would do honor to the most virtuous matrons on earth. Their teeth like ivory were regular and beautiful, without a single exception, and all of them, male and female, had the most marked English features. The clothing of the young females Consisted of a piece of linen, reaching from the waist to the knees þÿ and generally a sort of mantle thrown over the shoulders, and hanging as | low as the ancles þÿ but this covering appeared to be intended chiefly as a protection against the sun and weather, as it was frequently laid aside, and then the upper parts of the bodies were entirely exposed þÿ and it was impossible to conceive more beautiful form than they exhibited. They sometimes wreathed caps or bonnets for the head, in the most tasteful manner, to protect the face from the rays of the sun þÿ and though they had .only the instruction of their Otaheitan mothers, the dress makers of London would have been delighted with the simplicity, and vet elegant taste of these untaught children of nature. Continued from our last Their native modesty, assisted by a proper sense of religion and morality, instilled into their youthful minds by the patriarch Smith, had hitherto preserved these interesting people perfectly chaste and free from all kinds of debauchery. Smith assured his visiters, that since Christian's death, there had not been a single instance of any young woman proving unchaste nor any attempts at sedue. þÿ lion on the part of the men. They all labored while young in the cultivation of the ground, and when possessed of a quantity of cleared land, and stock sufficit nt to maintain a family, they were allowed to marry þÿ but always with the consent of Smith, who united them witti a sort of marriage ceremony of his own. The greatest harmony prevailed in the society. But what was most gratifying to the visiters, was the simple and unaffected manner ! in which they returned thanks to Almighty . God for the many blessings they enjoyed. þÿ They never failed to say grace before and after meals þÿ or to pray every morning at sunrise þÿ and they frequently repeated the Lords prayer and creed. It was truly pleasing says Capt. Pipon, to see these people so well disposed to listen to moral instruction, to belie v« in the attributes of God, and to place their reliance on Divine goodness. Only five ships passed within sight of the island from the date of the first settlement, in 1790, to the arrival of the Briton in 1814 of þÿ

tiiese only the Topaz and the Briton effected a landing. This is not surprising, considering the ruggedness of the coast, the total want j infant þÿ of shelter, and the constant and violent break- | ing of the sea against the clifls. The following petition for the admission of foreign suaar into the English rnatket for home consumption, has been numerously | s gned by þÿ wholesale and retail grocers, confectioners. and oth rs of London and its vicinity It sets forth þÿ þÿ That the importation of sugar from the I iritisri possessions in the West Indies has decreased to the extent of 40 000 tons, as compared with the average import of the ten consecutive years from 1830 to 1830, and 50,000 tons as compared with tint of the preceding years from 1820 to 1829 thus shewing a constant diminution during a period of twenty years ; and it is now ascertained that the deficit during the present season (1840) will be much more important. That the cultivation of sugar in the Island of Mauritius, appears to have reached its maximum. That the cultivation of sugar in Bengal has advanced more slowly than was anticipated when the equlization of the duty with that of Colonial sugar took place That the above are the only descriptions of sugar admissible for the home consumption of the kingdom. That this supply is inadequate to the wants of the population, vviio are compelled to pay an extravagant price for an article of great importance in culinary purposes, and essential to their comfort ; and of which the use might be almost indefinitely extended, if brought within the means of the lower and most exclusive class of consumers. That a high price for sugar, therefore, is an abatement of the comforts of the mass of population, and a hindrance and

From Bell's Weekly Messenger, June 27. COURVOISIER'S CONFESSIONS OF GUILT.

On Thursday night, when the additional evidence respecting the missing plate came to light, the articles so singularly discovered were closely examined by Sarah Muucell, the housemaid, and Ellis his þÿlordship late s valet, who at once identified the plate as his lordþÿship p s roperty ; but the iact of the finding of the articles was not disclosed to the prisoner until the following day (Friday), when Madame Ptolaine, mistress of the French hotel in Leicester- place, Leicester square, came to Newyate, and having seen the prisoner, with some other men, who were brought before her for the purpose in the Press-yard, she at once identified him as the man by whom the parcel containing the missing plate had been left at her house. The fact of the plate having been thus discovered, and the identity of of the prisoner proved, a communication to that effect was made to the prisoner, and on hearing a piece of intelligence so astounding and unexpected, the prisoner turned deadly pale and became extremely agitated, and before the time arrived for his being again placed at the bar, he sent for Mr. Flower, and at once disclosed to him the following confession ol his guilt: þÿ He stated that on the night of the fatal occurrence he was in the lower part of his þÿlordship h s ouse, in the act of secreting the different valuable articles described in tbe evidence on the trial, in the places where they were subsequently found by the police He then stated that his lordship, being taken sud-

denly ill, and coming down stairs unexpectedly while he was so employed, caught him in the act of concealing the property in the manner described. His lordship immediately charged him with robbing him, and declared that he would discharge him from his service on the following morning. Finding himself thus suddenly detected in plundering his master, and receiving notice that he would be discharged on the following morning, he was roused to a state of madness: and having wailed until his lordship retired to rest, he then stole softly into his bed room, and, finding that his lordship was sound asleep, he cut his throat with the very carving knife with which Mr. Holder so justly suspected that the dreadful deed had been perpetrated.

CONFESSION OF COURVO/dlER TO SHERIFF EVANS. The following is a verbatim copv of the confession made by Courvoisier to Sheriff Evans, as it was taken down on paper by the Sheriff: þÿ þÿ After I had warmed his þÿlordship b s ed, 1 went down stairs, and wailed about an hour, during which time I placed the different articles as they were found by the police. 1 afterwards went to the dining room, and took one of the knives from the sideboard. 1 then entered h s bed room, and found him asleep, I went to the side of the bed, and drew the knife across his throat. He appeared to die instantly. þÿ Francis Benjamin Courvoisier, þÿ Prison of Newgate, June 23, þÿ1840. þÿ This declaration was made before me this 23d June, 1840. þÿ William Evans, þÿSheriff

In the conversation which Sheriff Evans had on the day this declaration was made, and which lasted for an hour, the murderer assured the sherili that there was no truth in the statement that Lord William Russell had gone down stairs, and, after charging him with dishonesty, threatened to discharge him next day without a character. Nothing at all of the kind had occurred. His lordship never went down stairs in the night at all, and never threatened any thing of the sort. His lordship had certainly spoken to him in cross terms, and told him to be more attentive to his business ; but that was all. There was no further provocation.

saitsuI TJiOTiiraisx saorcnurar&s atot The sheriff having expressed some surprise at the variance between the two accounts, the murderer said that his uncle had entieated him most solemnly to tell the facts exactly as they occurred, and he determined to state nothing but what was accurately correct. He therefore acknowledged not only that he bad committed the murder under the circumstances just described, but that be had contemplated tbe murder aud robbery for a week previously. The she! iff questioned him a good deal upon the acknowledgement that he had so long contemplated the murder as well as the robbery, and he persisted in stating that tbe murder was premeditated, and not, as bad been previously stated, tbe suggestion of despair at loosing his character. He declared, and he wished tbe sheriff to let it be known to the world, that the idea was first suggested to him bv reading and seeing the performance o (Jack Sheppard. The book containing the history of Jack Sheppard had been lent to him by one of the servants of the Duke of Bedford, and he lamented that he had ever seen it.

The sheriff then asked him how Lord William þÿRussell finger s happened t<> be cut? þÿ The murderer replied tiiat when he drew the knife across the throat his þÿlordship s band started up as if by a convulsion, and must at the moment have come in contact with the knife, and immediately fell back again, for deaih was instantaneous : his lordship never woke. þÿ þÿHow, said tbe sheiiff þÿ did you get rid of the blood, for your band must have been bloody ?" Courvoisier replied that bis hand was bloody, but fie wiped it on tbe towel which be immediately afterwards placed over i Lamb and Flag publichouse, Cardiff, presenthis þÿlordship fact. s He then, he said, went up to bed, but he did not sleep. These were the strongest features of the conversation between the sheriff and Courvoisier.

HIS CONDUCT IN NEWGATE, & ATTEMPT TO DESTROY HIMSELF. Now that the jury have recorded their verdict against Courvoisier, we ate enabled to lay before our readers some additional particulars which may be relied upon fur their accuracy. On being taken to the condemned cell, on Saturday night, after the jury had delivered their verdict, the culprit appeared to be sullen and reserved, and he endeavoured to choke himself by cramming a towel down his throat; but his object writs happily frustrated by the vigilance of the officer in whose charge he remained. Before Courvoisier's conviction a French gentleman frequently visited him and administered to his spiritual comfort; hut since then the culprit has directed that his visits should be discontinued, alleging that he has made up tiis mind, and is quite prepared to die. In the course of Sunday and Monday the criminal repeatedly expressed a wish that his fellow servants might bo exculpated from the slightest blame, and he declares that the whole of their statements against him were founded in truth. There is one remarkable fact connected with tbe trial of the prisoner, and if the mistake had not been corrected, in all probability the ends of justice would have been defeated. The Lord Chief Justice, it appears, fixed Wednesday as the day on which the prisoner was to be tried, but his lordship afterwards found that that was the last day of term, and, in consequence of the judges being unable to attend, the trial was postponed until Thursday. Now, if this had

not been tbe ease, as one of the authorities observed, the additional evidence of Madame Piolane would not have been forthcoming, as Courvoisier was only identified by her on Friday morning, and inasmuch as trial would have been shortened, it is extremely doubtful if, on Thursday evening, it would not have ended in a verdict favourable to the murderer. The unhappy man appears in former life to have received a religious instruction, and in

J conversation with shows acquainted the that fie is tolerably well Holy Scriptures. The sheriffs have fixed Monday, the 6th of next month, for the execution of Courvoisier ; þÿ and upon the same day the next sittings of the Criminal Court will commence.

TRIAL OF OXFORD. The court on Monday morning was densely filled, immediately the doors opened at nine o clock, and several distinguished individuals were accommodated with seats on the bench, and in the watting þÿjurors box. At ten þÿo clock, Mr. Justice Tindal and Baron Parke entered the court, when Mr. S- Taj lor immediately rose, and asked the learned judges whether the trial of Edwaid Oxfoid, charged with high treason, might be postponed till next session, an application which he grounded on several affidavits, set. ting forth that material evidence could he procured on behalf of the prisoner. Inn that sufficient time hud not elapsed lor that purpose. After a short consultation between the judges, the application was granted, and the trial is consequently postponed till next session, which will commence on tiieOth ol July-

PROROGATION OF PARLIAMENT. Parliament was tliis day prorogued, with the usual ceremonies, by the Queen in person. Shortly before two o'clock, her Majesty, attended by Prince Albert, entered the state carriage, proceeded from Buckingham Pa- & lace to the House of Lords. As the Royal procession passed through the Park, and along the line of road, her Majesty and her illustrious consort were loudly cheered. The Ring and Queen of the Belgians were in the procession. The Royal cortege arrived at the House of Lords shortly after two o'clock, which was announced by a discharge of cannon. Her Majesty having robed, attended bv the Great Odi .-.era of State and the Household, proceeded to the house, and took her seat on the Throne, Prince Albert occupied a seat erected for htm on the left of the Queen. The entrance of her Majesty was announced by a flourish of trumpets. The Peers & Peeresses all rose as the Queen ent red. 1 fie house presented a brilliant spectacle. All the Foreign Ambassadors were present. I tie dresses of the ladies were very elegant. Her Majesty having taking her seat on the ihrone the Lord Chancellor directed Sir Augustus Clifford, Usher of the Black Rod, to summon the House of Commons to hear the Royal Speech on the prorogation of Parliament. The King and Queen of the Belgians occupied state chairs on the right of her Majesty. Her Majesty, who appeared in excellent health and spirits, then read with a clear and distinct voice the following most gracious Speech : þÿ

THE QUEEN'S SPEECH. My Lords and Gentlemen, The state of public business enables me to close this Session of Parliament ; and in releasing you from your attendance, 1 have to thank you for the care and attention with which you have discharged your important duties. ' 1 continue to receive from Foreign Powers assurances of then friendly dispositions, and of their anxious desire for the maintenance of peace. " I congratulate you upon the termination of the civil war in Spain. The objects for which the quadruple engagements of 1834 were contracted having now been accomplished, 1 am in communication with the Queen of Spain, with a view to withdraw the naval force which, in pursuance of those engagements, I have hitherto stationed on the northern coast of Spain. " I am happy to inform you that the differences with the government of Naples, the grounds and causes of which have been laid before you, have been put into a train of adjustment bv the friendly mediation of the King of the French. " I rejoice also to acquaint you that the government of Portugal has made arrangemeats for satisfying certain just claims of some of my subjects, and for the payment of a sum due to tins country under the stipulations of the convention of 18g7. " 1 am engaged in concert with the Emperor of Austria, the King of Prussia, the Emperor of Russia, and the Sultan, in measures

HJBhU3kittduaMfll unauit 'c ?3 .uw&».nMK« intended to effect the permanent pacification of the Levant to maintain the integrity and independence of the Ottoman empire, and thereby to afford additional security for the peace of Europe. " The violent injuries inflicted upon some of my subjects bv the officers of the Emperor of Cfiina, and the indignities offered to an agent of my Crown, have compelled me to send to the coast of China a naval and military force, for the purpose of demanding reparation and redress. " 1 have gladly given my assent to the Act for the Regulation of Municipal Corporations in Ireland. " 1 trust that the law which you have framed for further carrying into effect the reports of the Ecclesiastical Commissioners will have the beneficial effect of increasing the efficiency of the Established Church, and of better providing for the religious instruction of my people. " I have observed with much satisfaction the result of your deliberations on the subject of Canada. It will be my duty to exeeute the measures which you have adopted in such a manner as, without impairing the executive authority, may satisfy the best wishes of my subjects, and provide for the permanent welfare and security of my North American provinces. " The legislative bodies of Jamaica have applied themselves to the preparation of laws rendered necessary or expedient by the altered state of society Some of these laws require revision and amendment, but 1 have every reason to expect cordial assistance from the Assembly of Jamaica in the salutary

work of improving the condition and elevating the character of the inhabitants of that colony. The conduct of the emancipated negroes throughout the West Indies has been remarkable for tranquil obedience to the law, and a peaceable demeanor in all the relations of social life. " Gentlemen of the House Commons, of ' I thank you for the supplies which you have granted for the service of the year. " I lament that it should have been necessary to impose additional burthens upon my people hut I trust that the means which you have adopted for the purpose of meeting the exigencies of the public service art calculated to press with as little severity as possible upon all classes of the community. " My Lords and Gentlemen, "in returning to your respective counties, you will resume those duties which you perform so much to the public benefit and advantage. It is my anxious desire to maintain tranquility at home and peace abroad. To these objects, so essential to the interests of this country, and to the general welfare of mankind, my efforts will be sincerely and unremittingly directed ; and, feeling assured of your co-operation and support, 1 humbly rely upon the superintending care and continued protection of Divine i'rovidei/ce.'' The Royal procession returned to Buckingham Palace in the same order as it arrived at the House of Lords. Her Majesty was loudly cheered.

His Majesty received die members in the most gracious manner, and replied as follows : þÿ " Gentlemen. þÿ I thank you for the address you have presented to me 1 consider this day as one of the happiest of my life ; and my heart experiences great relief, because 1 know that tranquility and happiness arc restored to the country. 1 never doubled of this resuit, because during many years I have been able to convince myself of the loyalty, love, and devotedness of the Hauovarians to their dynasty. I knew that tliey would preserve these affectionate feelings towards me, because 1 never concealed my intentions towards them. God is my witness that I desire only the happiness of my subjects. The haps pincss of a Prince is inseparable from that of his subjects. Now that fhe now constitution is voted, a great object is attained, and you have worthily accomplished your task ; but no one can say that I, on my part, have not made all the eflorts of which I was capable. 1 have been directed only by the good of the country : and the nation will acknowledge, I hope, that my aim has been to establish its prosperity upon durable bases. Many things might have been better done, perhaps, but nothing is perfect in this world : nor can anv body act except according to the light he possesses. You have done your duty, and 1 have done mine. On returning to your provinces
you w ill reap the happy fruits of what w e have done for the good of the country. May God bless the country I"

There was afterward a grand dinner for 101 persons in the great hall of the Orangery at Herrerihausen, to which the members of the Assembly, the chief civil oflioeis, the court, the generals, and all the staff officers were invited, towards the end of the entertainment liis Majesty gave as a toast, " The Prosperity of the Country," in- a few words expressive of his elevated paternal sentiment. The Crown Prince gave " The King," which was received with enthusiasm. The King returned thanks, and said his existence here below was but from day to day. He xvas in God s hands ; Gut the country remained, and lie prayed the Almighty to lake it under his protection. It would be difficult to describe the deep impression made on the assembly by these words. On the day following the Assembly of the States was dissolved by Royal rescript.

From the St. Thomas Times, Wednesday September 23, 1840. The anniversary of our Most Gracious Sovereign's birth day on the 18th instant was ushered in by a Royal Salute from Christiun's-fort at sun rise. At 7 o'clock the Garrison and all the different Burgher Corps had assembled on the l'arade Ground and were reviewed by His Excellency the Governor. A general Levee, attended by ail the Civil and Military officers as well as by a great number of respectable Inhabitants, was held at Government house; where the wish of ' Long lite to our Most Gracious King Christian the 8th" was expressed by His Excellency, cordially joined in by all present and accompanied by lloyal Salutes from the Fort, and from H. B. M's Packet Pandora, Lieut, Innis, Commander. In the Evening very handsome Fire works were exhibited on the Parade Ground, provided by Captain Strandgaard, of the Royal Artillery. The joyous festival concluded on the following Evening by a general and splendid ball, given by H. E the Governor at Government house, enjoyed by a numerous assemblage of Ladies and Gentlemen until two o'clock the next morning. GOi) SAVE THE KING! -ocow þÿ From the Spectator, August 8.

POSTAGE BILL In aC Committee on this bill on Saturday, the Chancellor of the Exchequer was urged by Mr. Piiornely to allow merchants to send ship letters direct on board ship without passing through the Post office in cases where the ships sailed after the Post office was closed. 1 his, he said, would be a great convenience. '1 he Chancellor of the Exchequer was willing to accede to the arrangement, provided it did not open a door for fraud on the Post office þÿ So long as the Post office could do the business, he thought no other parties ought to be allowed to collect letters ; but he would permit merchants to avail themselves of the latest hour for sending those letters on board. When all the clauses of the bill had been agreed to, Mr. Warburton said, he could not allow the bill to pass without thanking the Chancellor of the Exchequer for having produced so unexceptionable a measure. He referred to the Post office returns to show what had been the effect of the reduction in postage- From these returns it appeared, that the number of letters sent by the London postage amounted previous to the alterations to 12,000,000 yearly, and that since the alteration it amounted to 23,000,000 ; so that in the London postage they had increased nearly in the proportion in which the rates had been reduced. The average charge on each letter, according to the old rate, was two pence and one third of a penny per letter ; it was now one penny ; and some allowance, in addition, ought to be made for the double and
treble letters, the number of which he belicv ed to be considerable. The annual amount of General Post letters, including ship letters and packet letters, had been estimated by the

®AW32R TOSVTOBaSK 3B2&»ai3EF&3 AT23. Post office Committee at 75,000,000. The annual amount at present was 127,000,000 ; therefore the increase fell little short of what had taken place in the London post ; and if they estimated the amount of revenue, taking in charges for double and treble letters, he considered the tesult to be most satisfactory. From the returns he saw a progressive increase ; in February the number of letters were 3,000,000 a week, and on June 22d the number amounted to 3,305,000. From that therefore, it would appear that there was a regular progressive increase every week. Nothing could be more satisfactory thairthe returns, and it was his firm belief that at no very distant period the returns would show as great an income as was derived under the old system of the Post office. On Tuesday, the bill was read a third time and passed.

The dates from China are to the 11th of April. The Chinese were actively engaged in making preparations of defence. Volunteers were invited and encouraged to join the Celestial army, and the women of several of the maritime cities had been removed into the interior from fear of an attack of the English. No hostilities had of late occurred along the coast ; except a brush between the Water Witch (which was at Macao on the 11th April) and some Mandarin boats Of the plan of operations nothing had transpired ; but it was generally believed that the campaign would open by the bombardment of Canton.

The great blow was impending þÿ not struck ; nor were the preparations for hostilities in so forward a state as to make it likely that the British forces would reach Canton in the month of May, as had been expected ; for the winds had been contrary, and the transports did not reach Penang till the 23d of April, w;hile Admiral Elliot only left the Cape towards the end of the same month. According to a letter in the Morning Post, from a commercial house in China, the uncertain position of the trade rendered it extremely probable that, after the shipment of twenty five millions of pounds of tea then lying at Canton, the market would be left bare even if the export were not interdicted. The intelligence from further India keeps alive the fear that our acquisitions in that quarter will be a mere addition of cost and trouble. According to some accounts, the Russians had reached Khiva ; ' and a though O Captain Abbot, our envoy, had passed on to St Petersburg with submissive overtures on the part of the Khan, it is not clear that the successes of the Russians had been so uncertain as to make them anxious to withdraw without full satisfaction of all their demands. The Foreign news of the week is of more than usual interest and diversity. The rumours current of the warlike disposition of France have received confirmation by the official publication of royal ordinances calling into active service 150,000 additional soldiers, and 10,000 seamen, five ships of the þÿ line, thirteen frigates, and nine steam ships. Anti alarmists say that these preparations signify nothing, for they are inadequate to carry on a war; but they are nevertheless strong precautionary measures towards a power with whom France is on terms of friendship. The French papers generally are less warlike in their tone ; but a strong feeling exists against England, for her presumed treachery. The explanation given by Lord Palmerston in the House of Commons on Thursday, meets a fractional part of the charge France was, it seems, fully informed of the steps the Allied Powers were about to take, and was invited and urged to the last to co-operate. M. Guizot, the French Ambassador in England, has been summoned to a conference with Louis Philippe and his Ministers; and his well-known moderation is expected to have a beneficial effect in smoothing existing asperities. þÿ Spectator, August 8.

The news of the landing and arrest of Prince Louis at Boulogne, reached Eu in the afternoon of Thursday, and was instantly communicated to his Majesty. The minister of justice immediately set off for Boulogne. The extraordinary attempt at Boulogne was beginning to excite more interest in Paris than at first seemed probable The King ieturned suddenly to that capital from Eu on Sunday morning, in order to assist at the deliberations of the cabinet on the subject, and determine on the course to be followed in respect ol the Prince and his companions. His Majesty was to return to Eu in the afternoon ol Sunday. T/ie Duke of Orleans, and other persons not members of the Cabinet, were present at the Council on Sunday, which lasied nearly lour hours.

On Monday the following ordinance appeared in the Moniteur : " Seeing that on August (J, an attempt against the safety of the State was made in the City of Boulogne, we have ordained and ordain as follows : þÿ ' Art. 1. The Court of Peers is convoked. The Peers absent from Paris will be expected to return immediately, unless good cause can be shown for their absence. " Art. 2. This Court will proceed without delay to the trial of the individuals who have been or shall be arrested as principals or accomplices of the above attempt." Arts. 3, 4, 5, and 6 provide the usual forms to be observed, the nomination of M. M. Franck Carre. Bomby, Nonguier, and Glandez to conduct the prosecution, and the Keeper of the Seals is charged with execution of the ordonnance. The news of these events was brought to Paris on Thursday morning by the telegraph. The government, as was its duty, immediately took means to ascertain whether the wild attempt of Prince Louis had, as it was welj warranted in supposing, any ramifications in Paris. In thecourse of Thursday and Friday morning several warrants were issued for the arrest of persons, and all of them wepe taken. Galignani adds that yesterday (Friday) some police officers paid a domiciliary visit to Madame Salvage de Fagerolles, formerly Lady of Honour to Queen Hortense, the Prince's mother, and who had tecently arrived from London, at No: 14, Rue de la Paix, where they seized a voluminous correspondence. From Boll's Weekly Messenger, August 1 1840. THE SYRIAN, EGYPTIAN AND EAST '- EliN QUESTIONS CONSIDERED.

in several of oui preceding papers we took occasion to mention the actual points and circumstances of the difficulty which has so long retarded the amicable and satisfactory settlement ot the affairs of the Pacha of Egypt and the Grand Seignor. It is in substance, that it is the established policy of the British government to maintain the integrity of the Ottoman empire, because such integrity þÿ we mean of course the retention ol all the territories which P at present possesses þÿ is necessary to qualify the Porte to keep up iis own independency, and thus to remain a principal empire in Europe. On the other hand, it has become the policy France, not only under the impulse ol ol certain Egyptian feelings which she has long been known to entertain, but, also as resp :cts the security of her knew conquests in Algiers, to take the part of the Pacha of Egypt, and to require that he should be allowed to retain Syria as well as Egypt, because, says the French government, Egypt without Syria will be unable to maintain herself, and m the first general European war will almost necessarily be seized upon by one of the belligerent powers. l'he first point which we think will strike upon the mind of every one is the admirable diplomacy ol Lord Palmerston throughout the whole affair. We shall not stop to notice the well known colloquial remark of Talleyrand, that an error in diplomacy is worse than a crime, but we shall stop to answer a question, which our readcts as well as our-

selves have often heard put ; þÿ with the real power of England what ought we to have to do with these devices of diplomacy at ail ? þÿ VV hy not rest upon our own independent strength, and leave foreign nations to settle their own quarrels and difficulties amongst themselves f The obvious answer is in the common maxim, that it is better to prevent than to cure; that it is safer and cheaper to prevent the occurrence of mischief, than to apply ourselves to remedy it when it has happened. The richness and greatness of Great Britain, our abundant resources, and our actual solid power, are the results of our commerce: and if we wish to retain this wealth and strength, we must be careful to keep open the unimpeded channel bv which it is fed and supplied. It is thus the first object of British policy to maintain and keep up her general commerce, and carefully to forestall and remove all obstructions which may be thrown in its way. Now, not only the quarrels of our neighbours, and the wars which may he consequent upon them, are the circumstances which constitute such obstructions, but still more so, perhaps are the particular treaties, into which one or other of those powers may be forced, either by becoming subjected to its enemies, or bv being brought into dependence by one or more of exported from Loudon and the its powerful neighbours. The object of an intelligent diplomacy is to prevent this mischief, and, under all possible contingencies to keep open the market to British commerce.
But to return to our more immediate point, the diplomatic management of Lord Palmerston and the singular, ability with which he fias conducted the department entrusted to him.

©AW31S. TiSMlTOlSS &IBt>r.B3OT03 ATI?. For the last ten years that we have watched Lord Palmerston, he has committed scarcely any but what may be called a venial error. In the Cracow question the embarrassment arose from the treaty of Vienna, and Lord Palmerston has done his best to get out of the late Lord Londonderry's entanglement. It is unquestionably a good and strong point to maintain in all cases the integrity of a sound political principle, and such is the principle of legitimacy, or that of supporting every nation in its ancient and admitted rights. But no human principle of mere prudence is universally true ; all of them admit of exceptions under the force of circumstances, and the independence of Cracow is one of that kind. þÿ It is not worth the cost of a war, to assert it. As regards the Spanish question, the conduct of Lord Palmerston, also, admits, of an obvious answer. The loan and the pecuniary advances made by Great Britain were a government affair, and not the act of the foreign minister. In the case of the blockade of Mexico, Monto Video and Buenos Ayres, he had no right to interfere as if it constituted a diplomatic question. It was purely an assertion of right on the part of France ; a right that the law of nations gives to every country which has to enforce a claim or to seek a compensation for any injustice. A blockade, bona fide must be borne by neutral nations, like all the other accidents of warfare, which press hard upon third parties. As regards the Eastern question, France,

as we have above said, has always aimed, in the first place, to carry out her own peculiar views, þÿ that of_uniting Syria and Egypt under Mehemet Ali ; and with this object, has always shrunk from signing any preliminary articles which the British minister has submitted to her ambassador at Constantinople. Under the able management of Lord Palmerston, France has in this respect been brought at last to a point. She must now either sign the treaty or not ; for the treaty is about to be concluded without her in case of further delays, and Lord Melbourne has expressly announced this resolution of the British cabinet in the House of Lords. The vexation of the Parisian radicals at this is extreme, but M. Thiers cannot any longer shift off the crisis. It is absurd to suppose that France will go to war upon this question with all Europe against her ; that she will resist a coalition of the united powers whilst engaged in the African war. She could not even desire to see Mehemet Ali compelled to submit hy the united force of the four allied powers. Whatever may be her augmentation of ioree, France is evidently on the check at this moment, and cannot escape with any honour. Her hankering after Egypt is effectually slopped.

The ceremony was conducted with their usual primitive simplicity and pious solemnity. Ills Excellency the Lieutenant Governor, attended by bis I'rivate Secretary, and accompanied by the Officiating Minister of this Parish, the Reverend R. H Barrow, the Rev'd. J. Cadinan (Weslevan Missionary) and the Brethren of the United-Church from their several districts, arrived on the platform which had been erected for the occasion, about 12 o'clock, where several public functionaries of the colony, including Members of the two Houses of Legislature, and a number of ladies and gentlemen, had previously assembled. þÿ pulmonary consumption, and with what «uo An immense concourse of labourers, from the

Mr. Ricksecker then delivered an interesting discourse from the words of the Psalmist, " This is the 'day, which the Lord hath made we will rejoice and be glad in it."

We were present on this very interesting occasion, and were much gratified not only by the spectacle, but by the reflections which the event naturally awakened in our mind. We there beheld many hundreds of our humbler brethren, who had themselves benefitted by learning the Commandments of God, assembled for the purpose of assisting to provide their offspring with similar instruction There also we saw the representative ol Majesty, the Parish Clergyman, the Wesleyan Missionaries, many of the influential persons and other ladies and gentlemen of our land congregated and harmoniously uniting with the Moravian Ministry, to promote the cause of our common Father. All differences whether in politics or religion appeared to be buried, and the feeling which seemed to pervade the vast mass, was "Glory to God in the highest, on Earth peace, þÿ good will towards men." Gomplexional distinctions, which are still too often exhibited in a greater or less degree at meetings in this Country, and which so much betray the minds that entertain them, were on Wednesday happily excluded. From the Philadelphia Inquirer of June 24. Important Surgical Operation for Consumption of the Lunga, There is no disease that has claimed and received a greater share of attention than
cess, the public is but too well aware ; any

remedy therefore that may offer but partial advantages in this fatal malady should be received with favor. We understand an operation was performed upon Mr. John Beitzel, of Kensington, on the 15th of May last, which promises entire success. The disease was in the right side, a great portion of the lung being occupied by an ahscess which communicated with the cavity of the chest þÿ lite diagnosis being based upon physical exploration. The operation was performed by Dr. J. P. Bethell, in presence of Drs. J. E. Taylor) J. k. Knorr, (J. Baker, G. W. Patterson, and T. A. Reilly. An incision was made about three inches long between the sixth and seventh ribs ; a gum elastic tube was introduced into the cavity of the abcess, and the pus drawn off by means of a pump. The orifice was kept open and the tube applied until the pus (which amounted to 24 ounces) was entirely removed. The patient immediately after the operation became entirely relieved ; his cough subsided, and his respiration became easy. He is now convalescent, having had no bad symptoms since the operation, and remains under the care of Drs. Bethell and Taylor.

We understand that Dr. Hamilton Carpcntier, the celebrated Oculist and Dentist, whose arrival in this Colony we lately noticed) performed operations for cataract on the eyes of an elderly gentleman, and a lady 63 years of age. He was assisted by Doctor Clancy- There were present on the occasion, Doctors Blair, Clifton, Vries, and Bascoine, who were all well pleased with the masterly and elegant manner in which the operations were performed. It must, of course, require some time to test their final success. This we intended to notice and remark on. þÿ Royal Cazette Denier ara August 31.

Royal Geographical Society. þÿ Soundings at Sea. þÿ At the last ordinary meeting of this society a letter was read from Captain James Rose, of Her Majesty's ship (Edipus, giving an account of some enormous soundings taken by him at sea. One of these, 900 miles west of the Island of St. Helena, extended to the depth of 5,000 fathoms, the weight employed amounting to 450lb. Another made in the latitude of 33 deg. S. and longitude 9 deg. W. about 300 miles from the Cape of Good Hope, occupied 49J minutes, in which time 2,266 fathoms were sounded. These facts were thought clearly to disprove the common opinion that soundings could not be obtained at very great depths.

The Farm of a Bonaparte. þÿ Mr. Hill, who has lately visited Bordentown and vicinity, says (in the " Visiter") that the premises of the late king Joseph, although he has been absent in Europe for the last few years, continue to increase in exterior beauty, as the grounds in useful cultivation must gain in annual production. The same buildings, whether of brick or wood, that were so trim and bright twenty years ago, lose none of their beauty and lustre. For more than a mile in distance, running alongside the old stage-road, and in sight of the present railroad, is the high picketed fence, through which is seen the margin of trees and shrubbery extending as a bank around the premises, and through that are descried the cultivated grounds, In one enclosure the deer are seen sporting along the trees þÿ in another is ground under cultivation ol the plough þÿ in a third is waving wheat, or other grain, or grass. Barns and other buildings are erected at suitable distance. The whole premises are laid out either for ornament or use of some sort. No part of them seems to be neglected. From this description it would seem, that some Republican farmers might take a lesson about the neatness, and the tin, ess of things, from this royal tiller of the þÿsoil. Boston Journal.

Admiral Baudin has resigned the command of the expedition to Buenos Ayres. Admiral M ackau is appointed his successor, and sails j forthwith. The latest accounts from the East state Mehemet Ali has agreed to secure the passage of the isthmus of Suez, to the English who are to occupy the ports of Mokka and Odeida. This news has been taken from a German paper, and certainly needs confirmation. Another rumour looks more like truth, which is that the Emperor of Kussia, about to renew the expedition against Khiva, has ordered the commanders to meet him at St. Petersburgh, the 3d of July, in order to take their instructions from his own lips The commanders of a new expedition against the Circassians are to be in attendance at the same time, and with a similar object.

PARIS, July 12. The Moniteur last night confirmed the news which I sent you yesterday, of the sudden change in the command of the naval expedition to Buenos Ayres. Admiral Baudin at the very moment of putting to sea, has either been deprived of his command, or has thrown it up for the reasons which I assigned yesterday, and Admiral Mackau takes his place. This affair has excited great interest, for the reputation of Admiral Baudin stands very high. He had taken considerable pains in making himself acquainted with all the bearings of the question at issue, and he and the minister parted upon a perfectly good understanding with each other. The affair appears to be involved in some mystery. Perhaps a clue may be found to it in the different title which Admiral Mackau bears to that which had been conferred upon his predecessor. In the words of the Moniteur, þÿ Admiral Mackau is named to the command of the naval division charged with the blockade of the Plata." The circumscribed duties implied by the former title, appear to imply a restricted command, such as Admiral Baudin, would not, at the 11th hour, consent to receive, and accordingly threw up the command.
