British and American Steam Navigation Company þÿ Ship President þÿ This ship will leave Liverpool for Now York on the 1st of August, and is undoubtedly the largest and most splendid Steam Ship that has ever been built- She measures 2,306 tons, and is therefore 350 tons larger than the British Queen, with which ship she is to keep up a monthly communication between this port, London and Liverpool, sailing alternately the first of each month The annexed particulars will give the public some idea of her arrangements, which are on a scale to reflect the highest credit to the enterprising company owning her. The accommodations for passengers in this magnificent ship are of the very first order combining the advantages of ample light, air and space, with the richest and most elegant decorations. The upper deck consists of a Saloon or Dining Room 34 feet wide by 28 feet long, communicating by a double entrance with a wide and lofty Corridor which reaches en-

tirely to the after part of the ship. On each side of the Corridor, are spacious State Rooms, for first class passengers, excellently lighted and ventilated, not entered as they usually are, immediately from the public walk, but from separate passages, each containing a large window. At the after end of this deck is a commodious room expressly for the Ladies' Room, and a large State Room lor a private family. The style of decorations of the whole is the Tudor Gothic of the 13th and 14th centuries. On entering the Dining Saloon from two lobbies, the appearance of it is very quiet and chaste. The panneling on all sides consists of Gothic work, richly carved, and painted to imitate new oak highly polished, the ground work of the pannels being of a simple neat color. The furniture is ail of real English oak, highly polished, with Gothic carving, and covered with embossed Utrecht velvet of a rich brown color. The dining tables are four in number, placed lengthwise of the ship, and when fully extended, will accommodate 120 persons to dine. The sofas are placed along the sides of the room, and at each of the four windows There are also four handsome Gothic sideboards, neatly fitted up, with a portrait of a þÿ President," (Washington being one,) over each. The whole, with the help of several mirrors, having an exceedingly light and elegant effect. The þÿLadies Cabin is also a very neat and elegant room, being richly ornamented in the Gothic style, in colors of white and gold, and

the wails hung with a pleasing imitation of tapistry of a grey colour, having the English rose and American star in neighbourly proximity. The Corridor, however, is the part, which for richness of effect and merit of design, exceeds all which we have hitherto seen on board any ship þÿ resembling rather a gallery in a nobleman's mansion. The ceiling, the lantern lights, the walls, and the doors are of the richest carved Gothic work, painted in imitation of old oak wainscoating ; and on both sides, the walls are hung with paintings (in imitation of ancient tapestry) on a rich crimson ground, representing the history and achievements of the great Columbus þÿ comprising all the most important events of his life; among which, (and not the least conspicuous) is his discovery of America. These subjects are extremely well designed and painted, especially when the difficulty of the imitation of needlew-ork is considered, and are all original compositions. It should be remarked, that the adaptation of the Gothic architecture of his time, and the story of Columbus, to a ship named the President and designed for the American trade, is in excellent taste. We would call the attention also, to the manner in which the introduction of light and air to the lower deck, is made ornamental to the corridor itself, by the introduction of a Parterre of flow ers, and an exceedingly light and neat spiral staircase which is the medium of communication between the two decks. The lower deck is laid out simply into

spacious, light and airy passages and state rooms, in which every contrivance for comfort which art can suggest has been attended to. The whole will accommodate 1 16 to 120 persons, and all so well that we should

be almost puzzled which berth to give the preference to. The whole of the fitting up, decorations and furniture are designed and executed by Mr. VV. B. Simpson, 459 West Strand, l.ondon, who also fitted up the British Queen. The following is a list of the subjects introduced in the Tapestry, No. 1, A. 1)., 1470. þÿ Columbus selling Maps and Charts at Lisbon, for the support of his family and aged father at Genoa. No. 2, A. D. 1470. þÿ Columbus contemplating enterprize, his is killed into enthusiasm by considering himself to be , the person alluded to in Holy Writ, who is to carry the Gospel into new lands. No. 3, A. 1). 1484. þÿ Columbus begging bread and water for his child at the Franciscan Convent of St. Rabida. Juan Perez Marcheza passing by, is much struck by his appearance. No. 4, A. 1). 1484. þÿ The conference at La liabida, at which Juan Perez Marcheza, and the Physician Garcia Fernandez, are struck by the grandeur of his views. No. 5, A. D. 1402. þÿ On Friday 3d August, 1402, Columbus set sail as Admiral of the Seas, and the Land be expected to discover. On the 11th October, Columbus stood on the stern of his vessel, when he espied land at 2 o'clock in the morning þÿ the foremost vessel then fired a signal. No. 0, A. 1). 1492. þÿ Columbus landed, and gave thanks to heaven for the success of his enterprize. At dawn, on the 12th Oct., he landed in the New Worid at Guanahain or San Salvador, one of the Bahama Islands, when the most mutinous ami rebellious of his crew thronged round him and embraced his

feet. The naked and painted natives regarded the white men as visitors trom the skies. No. 7, A. D. 1493. þÿ Columbus entering Barcelona in triumph. In his journey through Spain, he received princely honors all the way to Barcelona, where the Court then was ; several natives returned with him. No. 8. A. D. 1 193. þÿ Columbus received at Court by Ferdinand and Isabella, who rose as he approached, and raised him as he kneeled to kiss their hands.

No. 9, A. L). 1509. þÿ Columbus arrested, notwithstanding his great success; his enemies at home persuaded the king to supersede . him, and Francisco Boradilia was sent to I bring him back in chains. No. 10, A. D 1500 þÿ þÿColumbus arrival at Cadiz a prisoner chained, which event caused so universal a burst of indignation throughout Spain as to compel Ferdinand to disclaim all knowledge or share in the disgraceful transaction.
Columbus born 1419, at Genoa, died aged 61 years in neglect and poverty ! þÿ Thus \ ended,'1 says his historian, þÿ a noble and ! glorious career.

RELIGION OF THE CHINESE. According to Du flalde, the Ancient Chinese worshipped a Supreme Being whom they styled Chang Ti or Tien, which is said i be No: 1. ever after ; best attendance behind to imply the spirit that presides over the heavens, but in opinion of others is only the visible firmament. þÿ They also worshipped subaltern spirits, who preside over kingdoms, provinces, cities, rivers, and mountains. Under tins system, which corresponds With what is called Shammism, sacrifices were otlered on the summits of hills. About A. D. 95, the sect called Fo, was intioduced into China from Hindustan. The name was derived trom the idol Fo (supposed to be the Boodh. ol Hindostan), and the chief tenenls are those of tfie Hindoos ; among which is the metempsychosis or transition of the souls from one

B3AT13 animal to another. The Chinese are so far from being atheists that they aie in the opposite extreme of polytheism, believing even in petty demonds who delight in minute acta of evil or good. There is properly no order of priests, except the bonzes of the sect of Fo; this sect, and that of Lao Kian, which is the same as that of the Tai See ; admit of monasteries. Though the Chinese have no Sabbath, nor even such a division as the week, yet the temples are always open for the visits of devotees. But little has been done for the propagation of Christianity. The discovery of a conspiracy against the Emperor in 1823 gave rise to a general persecution of the Christians, which however, terminated in 1824. According to the accounts of the French mission in China, the number ot Christians in that country in September, 1834i amounted to 49.287 ; jtbere were twenty-seven schools for Christian boys and forty-five for Christian girls. In the year 1829, two Chinese Christians were brought to Paris : they spoke Latin as most Christians ,of that country do.

GOOD AND BAD NEWS. Bad News weakens the action of the heart, oppresses the lungs, destroys the appetite, stops digestion, and partially suspends all the functions of the system. An emotion of shame flushes the face ; (ear blanches it ; jov illuminates it ; and an instant thrill electrifies a mil. lion of nerves. Surprise spurs the pulse into a gallop. Delirium infuses great energy. þÿ the fulness of Volition commands, and hundreds of muscles spring to execute. Fowerful emotion often kills the body at a stroke ; Chile, Diagoras, and Sophocles, died of joy at the Grecian Gaines. The news of a defeat killed Philip V. One of the Popes died of an emotion of the ludicrus, on seeing his pet inonkev robed in pontificals, occupying the chair of state þÿ Muley Moloch was carried upon the field o battle, in the last stages of an incurable disease ; upon seeing his army give way, he rallied his panic stricken troops, rolled hack the tide of battle, shouted victory and died. The door keeper of Congress expired upon hearing of the surrender of Cornwallis. Eminent public speakers have often died in the midst of an impassioned burst of eloquence, or when the deep emotion that produced it had suddenly expired. Lagrave, the young Parisian, died a few months since, when he heard that the musical prize lor which lie had competed, was adjudged to another. The recent case of Hill ot New York, is Iresh in the memory of all. He was apprehended for theft, taken before the police, and, though in perfect health, men-
tal agency forced the blood from his nostrils, and he was carried out and þÿdied. Educational Mag.

From Bell's Weekly Messenger, July 11. EXECUTION OF COURVOISIER. FOR THE MURDER OF LORD WILLIAM RUSSELL.

CONDEMNED SERMON. On Sunday morning the Rev. Mr Carver, the ordinary of Newgate, preached what is called the condemned sermon in the chapel of Newgate. Immediately before the service commenced Courvoisier entered the chapel, attended by two of the turnkeys, and sat on a bench before the pulpit. He never once raised his eves during the service. In fact, his iooks denoted extreme sorrow and contrition, and he seemed to suffer great inward agitation when the ordinary particularly alluded to his crime. He was as attentive as possible to the service, and held the Prayer-book with a steady hand. The ordinary took his text from Job, chap, xxxiv , v. 21,22: þÿ þÿ For his eyes are upon the wavs of man, and he seeth all his goings. There is no darkness nor shadow of death where the workers of iniquity may hide themþÿselves. After Courvoisier left the chapel he was visited in his cell bv the Swiss Consul, who handed to him a letter from his mother, conveying her forgiveness, her blessing, and her farewell. He wrote with a steady hand a few lines in answer to the letter, and received a promise from the Consul that it should be delivered. The answer was an attempt to console the unhappy parent for the misery and disgrace which his crime had brought upon his family. He was subsequently visited by the Swiss clergyman, who had been frequently to see him since his conviction. Oxford sat behind Courvoisier, and between two turnkeys. He also seemed to pay attention to the service, and he sometimes joined

in the responses. When the ordinary was uttering the prayer for the Queen he looked up with a foolish grin, but immediately after resumed his attention to the service and behaved with decent seriousness.

EXECUTION. On Monday morning, at eight þÿo clock, F B Courvoisier expiated the guilt attached to his foul and heinous crime on the scaffold erected in front of the debtors' door at Newgate. On no occasion of a similar description for many years has there been created in the public mind so deep and painful a sensation as, the melancholy and appalling murder of Lord William Russell. A few minutes after six o'clock, the Rev Mr. C arver, the ordinary of Newgate, arrived, and immediately proceeded to the condemned cell, for the purpose of preparing the wretched man to receive the last rite prescribed by our church At seven þÿo clock, sheriffs Wheelton and Evans, attended bv their under sheiiffs, Messrs. France and Jackson, also arrived at the gaol. After the condemned sermon yesterday, the rev. chaplain visited Courvoisier in his cell, and again in the evening, staving with him a consider a f»le time. Courvoisier went to bed at eleven þÿo clock last night, and prior to doing so he requested the governor of the prison, Mr. Cope, to have him called at tour this morning.

He then dressed himself, and having washed, he requested permission to be supplied with pen, ink, and paptir, which was readily granted. He then employed his time in writing several letters in the French language until the arrival of the rev. ordinary. Alter joining in prayer for some time, the wretched culprit partook ot a slight breakfast. He appeared remarkably firm, and conversed with the chaplain and sheriffs freely He then partook of the sacrament in the presence ot the vast number of visitors who were permitted to enter the cell. His arms having been pinioned and the usual preparation made, the mournful procession moved from the condemned cell. Courvoisier looked exceedingly pale and wan but bis features bespoke the greatest complacency. He walked with a firm and dignified step across the prison yard, but on entering it the distant hum of the crowd for a moment appeared to unnerve him. He however instantly recovered, and resumed his fnm demeanour. The solemn procession then proceeded through the various avenues of the prison leading to the place of execution. On arriving at the entrance to the þÿdebtor d s oor, Courvoisier turned and bowed his head towards the sheriffs, and then, with amazing firmness, ascended the steps leading to the scaffold. On bis appearance on the platinum after the first great burst of indignation from the populace had passed, and the cties of

þÿ Hats þÿoil, had subsided, a dead and almost breathless silence prevailed. Courvoisier preserved his complacency and took his station with the same firmness he had exhibited throughout, under the fatal drop. He kept his eyes fixed towards the ground and showed no symptoms of weakness or emotion until the cap was placed over his face. It was then evident that a convulsive shudder was agitating Ins Iraine, but it was momentary, as scarcely an instant had elapsed before the signal was given and the fatal bolt was drawn, sending this guilty malefactor into the presence ol his Maker. The moment the drop fell the yell of the multitude ringing in the ears of the dying man was truly awful. He struggled exceedingly hard for two or three minutes, and the agonies of death caused his legs to be diawn up completely under him, indeed so much so, that the executioner was under the necessity of adding his weight to them in order to keep them down. Immediately the drop fell, the rush made towards the barriers surrounding the scaffold was tremendous þÿ the screams of the females awful. Many persons were thrown down and trampled on in a very dreadful manner. Courvoisier was attired in a black surtout coat, black trousers, and a marone-coloured satin waistcoat. He never spoke to the executioner, arid, after entering on the scaffold, appeared engaged in fervent prayer. During the time of the body hanging the scene in the Old Bailey was truly frightful, from the thousands rushing in adverse direc-

tions, and but for the excellent arrangement of the barriers a frightful loss of life must have ensued the 300 City police stationed round the scaffold being unable to do anything þÿ At nine o'clock the body was cut down and conveyed into the prison, where, during the day, a cast of the head will be taken, and the body buried to-night in the precincts of the gaol.

Upwards of 100 persons of rank and fashion obtained orders by admission to the gaol, among whom were observed Lord Alfred Paget, Lord Adoiphus Fitzelarence, the Earl of Chesterfield, the Marquis of Waterford. Sir George Oar roll, Alderman Gibbs, Alderman Magnay, Mr. Charles Ivean. & c. &c.

THE FINAL CONFESSION. On Saturday the prisoner wrote a very long confession, and delivered it to Mr Carver, the ordinary, and Mr. Baud, the minister of the French Protestant chapel in Threadneedle-street,. who afterwards read it over to him, and asked him whether it was all correct, to which lie replied that it was. They then asked him if there was anything that he wished to add to it, and he replied nothing whatever. The confession is wiitten in the French language, with a slight admixture of Swiss, which made it somewhat difficult to translate. We, however, have seen a translation of it, and which has also been read to to the prisoner, and acknowledged by him to be coirect. We were not allowed to take a copy of it, it being thought that it ought not to go fortii to the public until after the execution. The confession does not contain any fact with which the public are not already acquainted. It commences by stating, that he had planned the robbery several days before it was committed. It does not state (as in the first confession) that Lord William Russell come down stairs and caught him in the act of hilling some of bis Lordship's plate. This part is altogether omitted. After stating that he had resolved on the robbery, it says, he went up stairs to his þÿlordship b s ed-room, and finding him asleep, he went down and got a large carving-knife, with which he returned, and having tucked up the sleeve of his coat, cut his throat. It then gives a very long account of his having hid the different articles

lie had stolen, and persists in the statement that he Ind some of them w bile the police were present. It repeats the story of his having hid the 10 sovereigns in the cell at Bowstreet, and concludes by thanking the clergymen for the kind attention they had shown him It is written in a firm hand, all except the signature, and is attested by the ordinary and the Rev. Mr. Baud.

The Prince of Canino (Lucien Bonaparte) died at Viterl.e, on the 29th ult., at the age of 6(1. He was the second brother of Napoleon, and born in 1775. Exiled from Corsica in 193, betook partin the several phases of the French revolution, till he was created Munster of the Interior under the Consulate . he was subsequently ambassador in þÿSpai n, and employed in various confidential missions, till, quarrelling with Napoleon about his second marriage, he separated himself from politics. He was taken prisoner by the English off the coast of Malta, and fixed his residence at Ludlow, where he was much respected At the peace of 1814 he went to Home, but returned to Paris on þÿVapoleon s escape from Elba. After the final overthrow ofhis brother he retired to Italy, where lie passed the remainder of his days, devoted to literature and the fine arts, and was much respected in private life.

From Bell's Weekly Messenger, July 4. Besides the late India news, which arrived yerterday, and which will he found in another column, the only foreign intelligence of the week of any importance has been an unexpected movement of the Russian fleet which, it is apprehended, may be directed towards China, and which may thus be employed to embarrass our affairs in that region. The fact on which we build this remark is the following intelligence, stating that tbe St George Steam packet Company's steam-ship Sirius Lieutenant Waters R N., commander, which arrived off' the London Docks on Sunday morning, sailed from Cronstadt on the 19th ult. The Sirius, on proceeding up to St. Petersburgh on the 13th, between Revel and Helsingfors, passed through a Russian fleet of eight sail of the line (one a three decker), a large frigate, with a rear admiral's flag, and a corvette. They appeared to be working to the westward under easy canvass, and seemed to sail very unequally. When the Sirius left Cronstadt on the 19th, at nine p. m., theie were several Russian frigates and corvettes and one two-decker in the roads.

A Berlin letter stales that the late King left 30,000 crowns for the poor of Berlin. 5000 for those of Charlottenbourg, and 10,000 for those of Potsdam, Breslau, and other towns. His Majesty has applied 30,000 crowns for the improvement of the roads in the ancient March of Brandenburg, together with a considerable sum for the assistance of needy landowners. One million of crowns have been bequeathed for the improvement of the fortress of Posen. Another act of munificence does the greatest honour to the enlightened mind of the deceased monarch. By a private memorandum his Majesty has directed that a Catholic church shall be built, and in a marginal note are added the words, þÿ Let nothing be spared."

On Monday last, at the Durham sessions, Robert Taylor, one of the most impudent impostors that we ever remember to have read of, was tried for polygamy. The oflender is a mere youth, between 19 and 20 years of age, but his numerous matrimonial adventures and devices to obtain money, mark him as a person of singular cunning and dexterity. His plan seems to have been in all cases to of January, 1840, was 1 1,233,744 þÿgallons. practise first on the cupidity of his own sex, i by holding out a pecuniary reward to any one who would procuie him a suitable alii- i relating ance, and then, by representing himself to be j bert of aristocratic birth and heir to extensive possessions, to dazzle and win over the victim ai.d her friends. To aid his views ! he married he represented himself as a son of Lord Kenedy, of Ashby Hall, Leicestershire. He was furnished with numerous documents framed to corroborate his misrepresentations. These, which he carried in a tin case, were found on his person when he was apprehended Amongst them was a parchment, on which was written in a fine clerkly hand, what purported to be þÿ the last will and testament of Lord þÿKenedy, &c. es, Iplate, jeweller, a even ships. þÿ John Nicholsen, Thomas Johnson, & M s þÿRobinson appeared to have been constituted þÿ guardians of the said Robert þÿTaylor. The documents bore date 22d September, 1829, and exhibited the signatures, first, of the supposed testator þÿ þÿKenedy, and then of the attesting witnesses, Samuel Robinson, clerk to James Lee, þÿ and John þÿTurner, þÿand William Cowley, þÿbarrister. He had also an indenture certifying the correctness of the will, and describing his person by certain marks on his right arm, &ia. He had sundry other papers ingeniously enough contrived for the purpose of aiding his deception, but, as he is a youth of coarse and vulgar manners, the success which attended his impostures can only be accounted lor bv tire blind avarice of bis dupes. Up to tbe present time six of his mariiages, in several parts of the north of England, have come to the know ledge of the police, and there is reason to believe that the number is much larger. It is supposed that i he married one or two young women in this county.. Like many who have pursued a career of base and unprinciple deception, this scoundrel affected great sanctity, and connected himself at different times with both the Wesleyan and Frimitive Methodists. The object of this novel is to give notice to all young ladies and expectant coquettes that matrimony is a snare and a pit fall, that it brings nothing hut trouble and ill treatment, and that the woman who desires to secure ease and happiness must energetically make up her mmd to a state of single- blessedness, which, according to Miss Aylmer, is the only state of blessedness for woman The moral is þÿ Never marry ; or, in the words of some nameless doggerel, addressed with equal cogency to the other sex þÿ Fall on your sword, or on a rock ; Fall from some height above ; Fall from your horse, and break your neck ; þÿ But never fall in love.

Some of the critics, we perceive, have been praising this novel lor its þÿ sound þÿprinciples Perhaps they are right Married life is not calculated to produce happiness under any circumstances ; and the unfortunate people who imagine -themselves happy in wedlock, are merely the victims of self delusion. They are not happy, whatever they may think to

The þÿ sound þÿprinciples o (Miss Aylmer shew, as clearly as the sun at noon day, that there is j no such thing as contentment, or eveu securi- \ ty, in marriage. This Miss Aylmer is, ot ; course, the heroine of the story ; a clever, penetrating character, who makes deep reflections on the state of society, observing closely the conduct of all the people around her, and who may be said to dedicate her hie to the solution of the important problem. þÿ To marry or not to marry. þÿ All the married women with whom she is acquainted are miserable. Their husbands are all either þÿ brutes or þÿ fools. These discoveries, accumulating upon her quite shock her sensibility, and impress upon her mind a very horrid notion of men in general. But human natuie is human nature for all that, and Miss Aylmer two or three times þÿ þÿfancies herself in a fair way to be in love : but luckily, some fortunate revelations expose the iniquities of the ) objects of her transitory impressions, and she escapes miraculously from the dangerous temptation. Gathering wisdom from experience, she resolves to remain single, taking j this resolution at the age of twenty five ; Such is tiie þÿmoral and such are the" sound j þÿprinciples of this very curious novel. St. Croix Chuistiansted, Monday þÿSept br. 7, 1840 Some extracts from the London Times of Atigt 1st will he found in this þÿday G s azette. It would appear that a great war excitement prevailed at Paris the latter part of July, caused bv a þÿnew treaty between Russia, Austria, Great Britain and Turkey to support the last named power against the Bey of Egvpt þÿ France appears indignant, and evidently sides with Mehemet Ali. The latter has succeeded in landing a large additional force from Alexandria at Beyrout in Syria, thereby raising þÿIbrahim army s to 80.000 men. Admiral Napier with an English Squadron sent to watch this movement of Mehemet Ali, arrived too late to prevent it It is stated in the French papers that orders, have been sent to Admiral Stopford to capture Egyptian vessels. Tha Paris papers are full of warlike demonstrations against England and not sparing in abuse of Lord Palmerston. They slate that an addition of 200.000 men is to be made to the army, and all the ships of war, steamers dec. are to be immediately fitted out. This is probably gusconaite. as it can hardly be believed that France will embroil herself in war with the other four great Powers of Europe for the sake ol supporting the Bey of Egypt.- The three days Fetes the latter end of July, passed off peaceably at Paris, where the presence of a regular army of 00.000 men, united with the National Guards, overawed any insurrectionary movement. The latest advices from Spain are of an interesting nature The Queen and the Queen Regent had arrived at Barcelona, where Es-

partero had obliged the Regent to revoke a Decree by which the right ol suffrage in regard to Municipal corporations had been greatly curtailed ; Espartero also succeeded in obliging the Regent to name an entire new ministry of Liberal principles. Espartero ap. pears to be much blamed in the Paris and London Anti Liberal presses, where he is stiled a Dictator, Rebel &c., but supported bv a 100,000 victorious soldiers, the old veteran will probably carry his points. Cabrera has been sent to the castle of Ham, the late prison of Prince Polignac and his associates. There are no later advices from India by this Packet, nor any farther mention of the movements of the Russian fleet in the Baltin, The Earl of Durham died suddenly at Cowes Isle of Wight, the latter part of Julv, being on an aquatic excursion for the benefit of his health ; he was in the 48th year of hi age. The average price of British Island Mucoll vado Sugar, July 30th was 57s. 2d. in bond. Foreign Sugar had advanced Is a 2s in bond.

From the London Times, August 1, 1840, It will be seen by our summary of French news, and bv some extracts in detail from the French papers, that a great hubbub is geting up in Paris on the subject of the treaty for the settlement of the Turke- Egyptian quarrel. We confess we do not attach much importance to this violent explosion of parties evidently unacquainted with the real circumstances of the case. The point is, what better mode could the French Government suggest for the settlement of that question ; and what reasonable ground have the French Ministers of complaint that they were not asked to be parties to a treaty which, though it was known that they approved the principle oi it, various circumstances made it inconvenient for them to sanction by personal adhesion ? The treaty is no doubt a hazardous experiment : but it France maintains her good faith, and does not oppose a project the principle of wdiich she has more than once admitted to be politically just, the hazard becomes nothing. We cannot bring ourselves to suppose that ,V1 Thiers and his colleagues can recommend war to support the tyrannical and rebellious Pasha of Egypt. On the contrary, we anticipate a firm tesolve for the maintenance of that alliance which has so long subsisted between England and France especially when it is evident to everv man of common sense that this treaty can bring no advantage to England beyond that which will accrue to every other great Power by the conclusion of that war between the Sri, tax and his subject which has so long

disturbed and disquieted the east of Europe- We have received by the ordinary express the Paris papers of Thursday, with letters from several of our foreign correspondents. PRIVATE CORRESPONDENCE. PARIS, July 30. The fetes of July are over. They have terminated without any serious accident, but they have been attended with demonstrations of national feeling which it is said the Court regrets to perceive, or, if you will, to have provoked. The warlike tone of the Government papers to-day has produced on the funds a very serious impression. A species of panic has, in fact, existed throughout the business hours. J feel bound to state, however, tha persons really well informed have no expec" tation of anything in the shape of war unless new incidents occur to exasperate or to stimulate the vanity of the existing Government. It is pretty generally admitted, however, that an attempt to coerce Mehemet Ali, which must have been contemplated by the treaty of the Four Powers, would be admirably calculated to produce most untoward events.

The ninth anniversary of that most awful and tremendous visitation, the Hurricane of the 1 1th August, 1N3J, w hich reduced this Island to a heap of ruins, and a scene of appalling desolation, was religiously commemorated yesterday. Probably ten thousand individuals were assembled in the numerous places of public worship, most of them, we should hope, deeply humbled under a sense of their unworthiness, and thoroughly impressed with gratitude for their wonderful preservation when there seemed to he no hope of safety from the raging of the elements, and when human precaution was of no avail against the furv of the storm. We may not see such another instance of þÿGod correcting s hand such another hurricane may not he permitted by the Divine Ruler of the world to occur for many years ; hut may we not dread that þÿ His judgments þÿare 1 still, þÿ in the þÿearth are even now hanging over this land ? May there not be other manifestations of Almighty wrath and displeasure preparing in the Divine counsels to humble us vet more, and to try us, and to exercise our faith, and to shew us our utter inability, with all our ingenuity, and industry, to carry on our undertakings to a prosperous issue, when God is pleased to withdraw his assistance, and commands the elements to baffle all our care and toil At this moment the prospects of our agricultural prosperity are getting gloomy. Another disappointment to the hopes of the planter seems to threaten our land. 'The present state of

the weather is becoming every day more alarming. The rains last month had excited the most lively hope of bountiful crops of canes, corn, and provisions; but the long spell of dry weather since, and the violence of a fierce, scorching sun, are calculated to strike us with terror, lust we should he afflict-

In the interior of tlia island, we understand, that the plants still preserve their healthy appearance, but to wutdward and leeward we hear they are sobering severely from the drought. Last August was dry, but this is, as yet, more alarmingly so. A most beautiful looking crop ot Indian corn meets the eye in every direction; but at this critical period, when it is shooting bloom, this diy arid scorching weather will, vve fear, be fatal to its arrival at maturity We would venture to suggest, with ail deference to our Ecclesiastical superiors, the reading of the þÿ Prayer for þÿRuin. in our beautiful Liturgy.
